tasks.short: Hand out menus, answer guests' questions about menu items and recommend dishes or drinks when asked.

steps.what: Waiter hands out menus and drinks card and explains how the menu works
Guests read the menu and ask about menu items
Waiter answers menu questions from memory and the menu text
Waiter walks to the kitchen to ask about an item they cannot answer
Chef answers the waiter's question about the menu item
Chef writes dishes that have run out on the kitchen board
Waiter checks the kitchen board or till for sold-out items
Waiter recommends dishes or drinks on request, reading the guests' wishes

tasks.design: Keep one record per menu item (description, ingredients, allergens, pairing note) in the recipe system ({OTHER}) and show it on the waiter's handheld in the {OTHER} point-of-sale ordering screen, so most kitchen trips become a lookup. Sold-out flags set at the kitchen screen grey out items on the handheld at once.
tasks.previous_blocker: Dish knowledge sat with the chef and in briefings; handhelds showed only names and prices.
tasks.enabler_now: Restaurant tills and QR menus can show item descriptions and allergen data, and recipe tools hold that data per dish.
tasks.still_hard: Reading the guest and recommending well stays personal; the record is only as good as the kitchen keeps it.
tasks.human_edge: Reading what the table wants, suggesting with confidence and making guests feel looked after.

ambition.what: Guests who prefer to read item details and pairing notes on a QR menu in their own language before asking.

tasks.altitude: The waiter spends the same time at the table and less time walking to the kitchen; nothing changes in decision rights.

reach.learn: Whether the same item record with pairing notes serves the bar menu.

evidence.claim: A QR ordering menu linked to the restaurant till lets guests read item descriptions and allergen information, in Dutch among other languages.
A recipe management tool stores allergen and dietary data per recipe.
Sold-out flags set on a kitchen screen can grey out items on waiters' handhelds.

assumptions: Boundary: from handing out menus to the recommendation given; taking the order is outside.
Input contract: per menu item a description, ingredient list, allergen flags and pairing note, produced by the head chef in the recipe system; fallback is asking the chef.
Native configuration is tried first: item notes in the till and kitchen-screen sold-out flags.
Guest and chef time is outside the waiter's savings.
Answers from memory and recommendations do not change.
Input contract for s6: sold-out flags set by the chef on the kitchen screen (s8) as soon as a dish runs out, with about the effort of writing on the board; fallback is the board.
unknowns: Whether item records exist beyond name and price.
How often waiters go to the kitchen with questions per service.
research_questions: What share of guest questions can a written item record answer?

already_counted.description: Waiter looks up item records on the handheld for questions they cannot answer, instead of walking to the kitchen.

incremental.description: Waiter flags item records that are wrong or missing.
Head chef keeps item descriptions and pairing notes current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: item records cover few of the odd questions, so most kitchen trips stay and s4 keeps 70 (8.6); high: records answer most questions on the handheld (12.2).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Learn the day's specials at the briefing and tell each table about them, including when they sell out.

steps.what: Chef decides the day's specials, ingredients and prices
Chef enters each special once in the recipe system with description, allergens, price and portions
Chef checks the special records before they go out: names, descriptions, allergens and prices
Manager keys the specials into the till as menu items today; after the change the checked records flow into the till menu, the printed board text and the waiters' handhelds
Waiter attends the pre-service briefing and tastes the specials
Waiter writes the specials on the board, by hand, copying the chef's notes today and the printed text after the change
Waiter notes the specials for themselves: copies them onto a notepad today, reads them on the handheld after the change
Waiter tells each table the daily specials with price
Waiter returns to tables when a special sells out

tasks.design: The chef enters each special once in the recipe system ({OTHER}) with description, allergens and price and checks it; it then flows once into the {OTHER} point-of-sale menu, a printed board text and the waiters' handhelds. Sold-out flags from the kitchen screen reach the handhelds at once, so waiters stop offering a dish before the guest orders it.
tasks.previous_blocker: Specials change daily, and nobody wanted to re-key them into several places before service.
tasks.enabler_now: Till menus can take items from a recipe system, and kitchen screens can push sold-out flags to handhelds.
tasks.still_hard: Telling the specials well is part of hospitality; chefs decide late and change their minds.
tasks.human_edge: Describing a special so it sounds as good as it tastes and matching it to the guest.

ambition.what: Specials posted from the same record to the restaurant's website and social channels before lunch.

tasks.altitude: Nothing changes in decision rights; the waiter stops copying specials onto paper and knows sold-outs sooner.

reach.task: Tell waiting guests about the specials
reach.learn: Whether the board text and handheld view help hosts at the door.

evidence.claim: A QR menu linked to the till shows item descriptions and allergen information to guests.
Guests must be told about 14 allergens in unpacked food; spoken information is allowed if a notice says guests can ask.
Till menus can import daily items from a recipe system instead of manual keying.

assumptions: Boundary: from the chef's choice of specials to guests told at the table; taking orders is outside.
Input contract: special name, description, allergen flags, price and portions available, produced by the chef in the recipe system before the briefing; fallback is the handwritten board.
The chalkboard may stay hand-lettered for style, copied from the printed text.
Chef and manager time is outside the waiter's savings.

The briefing, telling tables and the hand-lettered board keep their full time. s3n keeps 50 because waiters read the specials on the handheld instead of copying them. s6 keeps 80 because sold-out flags stop most offers of a dish that has run out. The chef's entry and check (s1e, s1c) replace the manager keying the till.
Input contract for s6: sold-out flags set by the chef on the kitchen screen as soon as a special runs out; fallback is the chef calling it out.
unknowns: Whether specials are already keyed into the till as items or rung up as open prices.
Whether the kitchen uses screens that can set sold-out flags.
research_questions: How often does a table order a special that has already sold out?

already_counted.description: Waiter reads the specials and allergens on the handheld before service instead of copying them onto a notepad.

incremental.description: Waiter checks the printed board text matches the briefing and reports changes.

approvals.approved_version: The day's special records with names, descriptions, allergens and prices exactly as checked by the chef in s1c, sent once to the till menu, the printed board text and the waiters' handhelds for that day; any change needs a new check.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the chef enters specials late, so waiters still copy many onto a notepad and sold-out flags come late; s3n keeps 80 and s6 keeps 95 (1.1); high: specials are in before the briefing and flags are set at once (4.5).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Explain to guests how dishes are prepared, which ingredients they hold and what allergens they contain.

steps.what: Guest asks how a dish is made or whether it holds an allergen
Waiter explains ingredients and cooking method from memory
Waiter looks up allergens in the paper allergen folder
Waiter asks the chef when the folder is unclear or the dish changed
Chef checks the recipe and answers the preparation question
Waiter tells the guest and adds an allergy note to the order

tasks.design: Recipe records in the recipe system ({OTHER}) hold ingredients, method notes and the 14 allergen flags per dish and feed a handheld view with a filter such as 'free of nuts'; a dish whose allergen fields are incomplete, or whose recipe changed since the chef last confirmed it, shows 'ask the chef' instead of an answer. Allergies are added as fixed modifiers in the {OTHER} point-of-sale order instead of free text, printed on the kitchen ticket; adding them takes as long as today.
tasks.previous_blocker: Allergen matrices were kept as paper or document files that fell behind recipe changes, and tills took only free-text notes.
tasks.enabler_now: Recipe tools store allergen data per recipe, and tills support fixed allergy modifiers.
tasks.still_hard: Cross-contact in the kitchen and supplier changes in ingredients are not in any record; a wrong answer can harm a guest.
tasks.human_edge: Taking an allergy seriously, judging when to fetch the chef and explaining a dish so it sounds appetising.

ambition.what: Guests with several allergies who can check a full list of safe dishes before they book.

tasks.altitude: The waiter answers more allergen questions directly and fetches the chef only for gaps; the chef owns the allergen record.

reach.task: Keep recipes and allergen data current when ingredients change
reach.learn: How often recipe changes are not reflected in the allergen record.

evidence.claim: A recipe management tool stores allergen and dietary data per recipe.
A QR menu linked to the till shows allergen information per item.
Businesses must inform guests about 14 allergens in unpacked food; spoken information is allowed with a notice that guests can ask.
In 2022 only 41% of 9,407 inspected Dutch hospitality businesses complied with allergen information rules.

assumptions: Boundary: from the guest's question to the answer given and any allergy noted on the order; the order itself is opened in the order-taking task.
Input contract: per dish the ingredient list, 14 allergen flags, method note and date of the chef's last confirmation, produced by the head chef in the recipe system; fallback is asking the chef.
No model writes answers: the view shows only what the record holds.
Chef and guest time is outside the waiter's savings.

Explaining from memory, telling the guest and adding the allergy note keep their full time. s3 keeps 50 because the handheld view and filter replace paging through the folder. s4 keeps 40 because the chef is asked only for dishes shown as 'ask the chef'.
unknowns: Whether the kitchen keeps recipes in a system or on paper.
Whether the till supports fixed allergy modifiers.
research_questions: How often does the allergen record lag behind a recipe or supplier change?

incremental.description: Waiter reports allergen questions the record could not answer.
Head chef confirms allergen data after each recipe or supplier change.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: the kitchen changes dishes often, so many records show 'ask the chef'; s3 keeps 70 and s4 keeps 75 (9.3); high: records are confirmed after each change (19.6).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

tasks.short: Help the host: take phone reservations and takeaway orders, greet and seat guests, thank them on leaving.

steps.what: Guest phones to book a table or order takeaway
Guest books a table or orders takeaway online, typing name, time, party size, notes or items themselves
Waiter answers the phone and checks table availability in the reservation system
Waiter enters the reservation: name, time, party size, phone, notes
Waiter writes the takeaway order and keys it into the till
Waiter greets arriving guests, finds the reservation and seats them
Waiter thanks guests and says goodbye as they leave

tasks.design: Configure the online booking widget of the reservation system ({OTHER}) on the website ({CMS}) with table rules and automatic confirmations, and an online takeaway order page that drops paid orders into the {OTHER} point-of-sale system and the kitchen screen. Guests who book or order online type their own details (s1o, guest time). Phone calls stay for guests who prefer them, large groups and special requests; greeting, seating and thanking do not change.
tasks.previous_blocker: Small restaurants ran on a paper book and the phone; online channels charged per booking or did not link to the till.
tasks.enabler_now: Reservation systems include booking widgets with rules, and ordering services pass orders and payment straight to the till.
tasks.still_hard: Older guests and groups keep calling; online bookings with free-text notes still need reading, and no-shows rise with easy booking.
tasks.human_edge: Welcoming guests, judging the right table for the mood and the party, and parting warmly.

ambition.what: Guests who book or order after closing time, when nobody answers the phone.

tasks.altitude: The waiter spends less time at the phone during service and the same time with guests at the door.

reach.task: Plan the table layout for the evening's reservations
reach.learn: Whether booking rules in the system replace the host's paper table plan.

evidence.claim: A Dutch ordering service takes orders and payment by QR code and passes them to several restaurant tills.
Reservation systems offer website booking widgets with table rules and automatic confirmations.
Allergy or health notes in a reservation are health data under GDPR and need a clear purpose and limited retention.

assumptions: Boundary: from the guest's call to the guest leaving; table service and payment are outside.
Input contract: booking with date, time, party size, name, phone and note, produced by the guest online or by the waiter by phone; fallback is the phone.

Scenario: 40 to 50% of bookings and takeaway orders move online in a restaurant with a website; s2 and s3 keep 55 and s4 keeps 50 for the calls and orders that stay by phone. The guest's own booking and ordering is shown as s1o and priced as customer time.
Native configuration is tried first: the reservation system's widget and the till's online order link.
Greeting, seating and thanking are unchanged.
unknowns: Whether the restaurant already has a reservation system or a paper book.
What share of guests would book online.
research_questions: Do no-shows rise after online booking, and does a deposit or reminder offset it?

incremental.description: Waiter reads online booking notes and handles changes and no-show follow-up.
Manager keeps table rules, opening times and the online menu current.

time_saved_range_pct.basis: Low: regulars keep phoning and only about 20% of bookings and orders move online, so s2, s3 and s4 keep 80 (8.5); high: 45 to 50% move online as assumed (21.8).

tasks.savings_basis: 100 focal-role baseline hours; external labour excluded; incremental focal work deducted once; provisional

role.altitude: The waiter keeps the table: welcoming, explaining, recommending. Kitchen trips for facts, copying specials and phone bookings shrink.
reach: Hosts' table planning from the reservation system
Cooks' upkeep of recipe and allergen records
skills_to_grow: Using the item and allergen record confidently with guests
Spotting gaps in the record and reporting them
role.ambitious_version: A waiter who answers almost every dish and allergen question at the table from a trusted record and spends the time saved on the guests.
